claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution with relatively uniform elemental distribution.
The initial state contains no discernible intermetallic precipitates.
High-temperature exposure enhances atomic diffusion in the Mg-containing alloy.
Thermal exposure causes diffusion-controlled decomposition of the metastable solid solution into a Mg-depleted matrix and Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The rates of precipitate nucleation and growth determine whether the Mg-rich intermetallic dispersion remains fine and coherent or becomes coarse and incoherent.
Precipitate size, distribution, and interfacial coherency mediate the continuity and protective character of the oxide scale.
Fine, coherent Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates can seed formation of a continuous protective oxide scale.
Fine, coherent Mg-rich precipitates will retain or improve high-temperature oxidation resistance relative to the initial state.
Fine, coherent Mg-rich precipitates will retain or improve corrosion resistance relative to the initial state.
Coarse, incoherent intermetallic precipitates interrupt protective-oxide continuity and diminish oxidation resistance.
Coarse, incoherent intermetallic precipitates diminish corrosion resistance.
Temperatures at or above 800 °C define the relevant high-temperature service regime in which intermetallic coarsening affects oxide-scale formation.
Chloride-containing media represent a relevant corrosive service environment for the proposed Mg-containing alloy.
The controlled comparison consists of specimens aged at 850–900 °C for multiple durations and specimens retained in the as-quenched state.

The mechanism is falsified if aging produces no measurable Mg-rich intermetallic formation or growth, or if intermetallic evolution has no measurable association with oxidation or corrosion resistance relative to the control.
